Patient Records Cloud Migration

A phased, safety-led transition to a secure and resilient cloud platform

Planning assumptions and estimates for executive review · 23 November 2026

Background

The hospital depends on its patient records system for clinical care, coordination and operational reporting. Aging infrastructure, growing data volumes and increasing recovery and security demands can make an on-premises environment costly to maintain and difficult to scale. A carefully governed cloud migration offers an opportunity to improve resilience, support access to records and modernize operations without compromising patient safety.

This proposal assumes an existing electronic health record (EHR) and associated interfaces will move to a vendor-supported cloud environment. The hospital’s architecture, contract terms, data volumes and regulatory obligations must be confirmed during discovery; cloud suitability and the migration approach are not presumed.

Objectives and acceptance measures

  • Preserve clinical safety and continuity: migrate agreed record sets and demonstrate 100% reconciliation of critical record counts, with no unexplained discrepancies in sampled clinical content before cutover.
  • Protect patient information: apply role-based access, multifactor authentication, encryption, audit logging and documented contractual and regulatory controls before production use.
  • Improve resilience: agree recovery time and recovery point objectives during discovery and demonstrate them in a restoration exercise before go-live.
  • Maintain service performance: establish baseline response times and availability, then meet hospital-approved targets in production-like testing.
  • Enable adoption: train all identified affected users before their cutover and obtain clinical and operational sign-off on workflows, downtime procedures and support readiness.

Specific thresholds, sampling methods and accountable approvers will be documented in the project charter.

Scope

Included

  • Inventory of patient records, dependencies, data quality, interfaces and applicable retention and residency requirements.
  • Selection and configuration of a vendor-supported cloud landing zone, identity controls, monitoring, backup and recovery.
  • Migration of agreed active and historical records, attachments and metadata; mapping, cleansing, reconciliation and clinical validation.
  • Remediation and testing of agreed interfaces, including laboratory, imaging, pharmacy and billing connections where present.
  • Security and privacy assessments, vendor agreements, user training, cutover, rollback planning and a post-go-live stabilization period.

Excluded unless separately approved

Replacing the EHR with a new product, broad clinical workflow redesign, unrelated application migrations, hospital-wide device upgrades and decommissioning legacy systems before retention and legal obligations are satisfied.

Key dependencies: EHR vendor support and licensing, cloud and network capacity, access to accurate data inventories, clinical staff availability, third-party interface cooperation and approval of the target jurisdiction and contracts.

Phased timeline

Illustrative 12-month schedule from authorization; phases overlap where practical. Dates and milestones will be baselined after discovery.

PhaseTimingKey activities and gate
1. Discover and planMonths 1–2Inventory systems and interfaces, assess data and risks, confirm requirements and costs. Gate: charter and migration strategy approved.
2. Design and procureMonths 2–3Confirm vendor support, contracts, architecture, residency and recovery targets. Gate: design and agreements approved.
3. Build and secureMonths 3–5Configure infrastructure, network, identity, logging and backups; prepare interfaces and migration tooling. Gate: environment ready for testing.
4. Migrate and integrateMonths 5–8Run test migrations, cleanse and reconcile records, adapt interfaces and rehearse recovery and rollback. Gate: data and integration testing accepted.
5. Validate and prepareMonths 8–10Complete clinical, security, performance and disaster-recovery testing; train users and rehearse cutover. Gate: clinical, security and operational go/no-go approval.
6. Cut over and stabilizeMonths 11–12Execute approved cutover, verify records and interfaces, provide enhanced support and hand over operations. Gate: service acceptance and project closure.

At the go/no-go gate, unresolved safety-critical defects, failed reconciliation or an untested rollback trigger postponement. Clinical leadership approves any downtime window and contingency procedures.

Planning estimate in USD for the 12-month project; not a vendor quotation. Amounts require refinement following inventory, procurement and contract review.

Base subtotal$1,400,000

Assumes existing EHR licensing and routine hospital staffing continue outside this incremental budget; costs of additional licenses, taxes, major hardware upgrades and early termination fees are excluded pending due diligence. The cloud line covers project-year consumption only; a provisional $180,000 per year thereafter is an operating-cost placeholder, not included in the project total, and will vary with usage and support arrangements. Avoided on-premises costs are not netted against this request.

Team roles and governance

RolePrimary responsibility
Executive sponsorOwns the business case, funding, escalations and final project accountability.
Project managerManages schedule, budget, dependencies, reporting and change control.
Clinical lead and representativesDefine safety requirements, validate records and workflows, approve downtime and clinical readiness.
Cloud / infrastructure leadDesigns and operates the cloud, networking, backup, recovery and observability.
Data migration and integration leadsOwn mapping, transfer, reconciliation and interface remediation and testing.
Security, privacy and legal leadsAssess controls, regulatory obligations, vendor agreements, incident response and data handling.
EHR and cloud vendorsProvide supported configurations, specialist implementation and contracted support.
Training and service operations leadsCoordinate communications, training, service desk readiness and operational handover.

A steering committee chaired by the sponsor meets at least monthly and at decision gates; it resolves escalations and approves material scope or budget changes. Clinical, security and operations leads jointly recommend go/no-go to the sponsor.

Risks and mitigations

RiskMitigation and owner
Missing or incorrect patient data affects careProfile and cleanse data; run repeatable reconciliation and clinically led sampling; block cutover on unresolved discrepancies. Owner: data lead and clinical lead.
Outage or failed cutover disrupts careRehearse cutover and rollback, verify backups, establish downtime workflows and maintain legacy access until acceptance. Owner: infrastructure and clinical leads.
Privacy breach or noncomplianceAssess applicable law and residency; execute required vendor agreements; enforce least privilege, encryption, audit and incident-response controls. Owner: security and privacy leads.
Interfaces or application performance failInventory dependencies early; involve vendors; test end-to-end workflows and performance against agreed baselines. Owner: integration lead.
Costs or schedule exceed planValidate estimates and contracts, track consumption and dependencies, maintain contingency and require change approval. Owner: project manager.
Users are unprepared for new proceduresEngage clinical champions, train by role, rehearse downtime procedures and provide enhanced go-live support. Owner: training and clinical leads.

Call to action

Approve the project in principle and authorize the $1.54 million planning envelope, subject to a refined business case and staged release of funds. Appoint an executive sponsor, clinical lead and project manager, and convene the steering committee to begin discovery.

First decision gate: At the end of discovery, review the validated inventory, vendor support, regulatory assessment, target architecture, baseline budget and schedule. Proceed to procurement and build only after the steering committee approves the revised plan.

Prepared for hospital leadership · Estimates and assumptions are illustrative and require local validation.
